description:
I'm high school student passionate about physics, AI, and NASA open data.

Previously, I participated in the SCO Young Scientists Camp, where we worked on a scientific paper about exoplanet detection using NASA datasets. Now we want to take on the Flame in Freefall challenge — building an AI-powered tool that helps understand fire behavior in microgravity and improve fire safety for future space missions.
summary:
MoleSkill is a web navigator for NASA's research on combustion in microgravity. Fire behaves differently in space: flames burn as spheres, and new environments such as lunar bases bring different oxygen and pressure conditions. Yet the relevant NASA experiments are scattered across archives and documents.
We built a tool that ranks 23 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics records for four mission scenarios (ISS, lunar base, pressurized rover, researcher) using six adjustable criteria, and links every fact to its DOI or to the exact page of 7 NASA PDFs. An AI assistant answers questions only from these documents: each answer must cite retrieved passages, and any answer whose citations or numbers cannot be verified is replaced by exact NASA quotes. MoleSkill also shows where data is still missing, such as combustion in partial gravity (Moon, Mars).
It is not a fire-risk simulator. It helps mission planners, safety engineers and researchers find and verify the right NASA evidence faster.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MoleSkill is a web navigator for NASA's research on combustion in microgravity. A user picks a mission scenario (ISS, lunar base, pressurized rover or researcher) and gets a ranked list of NASA experiments relevant to it. Every fact opens its primary source: the DOI of a NASA PSI record or the exact page of a NASA PDF. Users can compare 2-3 studies, adjust the weight of six criteria (prevention, high oxygen, detection, suppression, data for models, new controls), export the ranking as CSV, and see how studies are linked (reflights, ground work built on flight data). An AI assistant answers questions in English or Russian using only NASA documents.

HOW IT WORKS

The knowledge base holds 23 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics records (22 fire-safety core records) and 7 NASA PDFs (28 indexed pages). Search is a BM25 retrieval engine we implemented ourselves. Each record has 0-5 relevance ratings on six criteria; scenario weights turn them into a 0-100 score. For a question, the system retrieves the best matching record descriptions and PDF pages and sends only those passages to a Groq-hosted model (openai/gpt-oss-120b). The answer is accepted only if every citation points to a passage that was actually provided and every number appears in those passages. Otherwise MoleSkill shows exact NASA quotes instead of generated text. A FLEX checker compares oxygen and pressure with the ranges stated in the FLEX document (10-50% O2, 0.5-1.0 atm).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

NASA's combustion research is scattered across records and documents. MoleSkill lets mission planners, safety engineers, students and researchers find the relevant experiments in minutes and verify each claim themselves. It also shows where evidence is missing: PSI has no combustion data yet for partial gravity (Moon, Mars), which matters for lunar bases.

WHAT MOLESKILL IS NOT

It is not a fire simulator or risk forecast. The ratings are relevance ratings written from PSI descriptions, not NASA measurements, and oxygen and pressure numbers are confirmed by a document only for FLEX. The interface says so explicitly.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, python-dotenv, plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript with SVG charts, Groq API, 16 automated tests (pytest), SHA-256 manifest to verify data files, deployed on Vercel. No special hardware.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most AI tools answer first and cite later. MoleSkill reverses this: retrieval comes first, and a generated answer must pass a citation and number check or it is discarded. The project also treats missing data as a result, not a failure. Its identity comes from the science: in microgravity flames burn as spheres, which became our logo and visual style.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about limits (no invented numbers, no risk claims); source traceability (every fact links to a DOI or PDF page); data integrity (the PDF files had names that did not match their content, so we matched them by the title on the first page and documented this); security (the API key stays on the server); and NASA branding rules (no NASA logos or identifiers are used).
